title: Forty minutes, first activity
setting: Two teachers compare notes after a lesson that went off plan.

lines.t: The lesson plan said forty minutes for the whole thing.
And?
The warmer took forty minutes. They were actually talking, so I let it run.
That's the right call. What got cut?
The drill and half the handout. The syllabus says we finish the unit today, and the syllabus has never met this group.
Do the drill on Thursday. They'll need it more after they've tried to use it.
It's a mixed-ability class, so the drill helps the quiet three and bores the front row.
Then put the front row in pair work with them. Everybody gets something.
And the recap?
Five minutes at the start, always. Half of them were mentally on the bus last week.

title: She missed three weeks
setting: A teacher and the head talk about a student who disappeared and came back.

lines.t: Milena is back. She missed three weeks.
Her attendance was perfect before that. What happened?
A project at work. She assumed she was too far behind to return.
That's how most of our drop-out rate happens, and it's never about the English.
She caught up in one lesson. It was slightly annoying for everyone else.
Put that in her progress report, in those words. She'll read it twice.
She's hit every learning objective from the weeks she missed. I checked them one by one.
Write that down as well. People believe a tick more than a compliment.
Should I offer her a one-to-one to fill the gaps?
Offer it, don't push it. She doesn't have a gap, she has a memory of having one.
And the placement test from September?
It put her one level too low, like it does with half the confident ones. Move her up in January.

title: Week six is always optimistic
setting: Two teachers argue with the syllabus before a new intake starts.

lines.t: The September intake starts in three weeks. Is the curriculum still right?
Mostly. The module order is fine. The syllabus promises the past perfect in week six.
And week six is always optimistic.
Every year. They're still fighting the past simple, and we hand them a second past.
How many contact hours before that point?
Eighteen. It sounds like a lot until you spread it over six weeks.
What if we move it to week nine and give week six to self-study?
Self-study only works if somebody checks it. Otherwise it's a week of nothing with a nice name.
Then blended learning, the honest kind: one lesson, one online task, and I look at the task.
That works. And put B1 as a prerequisite in writing, because people read it as a suggestion.

title: The tenth was sent by their employer
setting: The head and the office manager look at why January works and February doesn't.

lines.t: Enrolment is up 40% on January. It's up every January.
The whole country briefly believes in itself. Then February arrives.
What actually converts them? Admissions has the numbers.
The trial lesson. Nine of ten who take one sign up.
And the tenth?
Was sent by their employer and didn't want to be there in the first place.
And the open day in September?
The open day fills the room with people who came for the coffee. Two of them enrol, so we keep doing it.
Then push the trial lesson harder than the tuition fee.
Agreed. Nobody argues about the fee anyway, they argue about paying it all at once.
So offer the instalment plan by default rather than on request.
And publish the term dates in June. Parents plan holidays before we plan lessons.

title: Three empty rooms at ten
setting: A conversation about money that turns out not to be about students.

lines.t: Fee income looks healthy in October and lonely in July.
That's the shape of this business. What's worrying you?
Three empty rooms at ten in the morning, every weekday.
Everybody wants six o'clock, so we fight over six o'clock.
That's a utilisation problem, not a marketing one.
Then a daytime rate. Shift workers, parents on leave, people who've retired.
Class size can go to ten in the daytime. The rooms take twelve.
Who covers those hours? The timetable is finished on Friday and wrong by Monday.
I'll teach two of them myself. The head teacher should be in a classroom somewhere.
Put it in writing before the inspection. Accreditation people love a head teacher who still teaches, so let them love us.

title: Fifty-nine
setting: Marking is finished and one result needs a decision.

lines.t: Marking's done. The end-of-term assessment took the whole evening I was planning to have.
It always does. Any surprises?
One. The pass mark is 60 and Stoyan got 59.
He'll remember that number for years. Everybody does.
Do I round it?
No. Offer the resit and tell him what the missing point was, in one sentence.
He'll ask about the certificate before he asks about the mistake.
They all do. The certificate comes with the grade, the grade comes with the resit.
It was the writing task. He answered a different question.
Then he'll pass the resit. The resit group is always better prepared than the first sitting.
And the mock exam? Half of them skipped it.
Make it compulsory. The mock exists so the real one is the second time, not the first.

title: The photocopier is down
setting: Eight fifty-five in the staff room, the way it goes every week.

lines.t: The photocopier is down.
Of course it is. I have twelve handouts and eleven minutes.
Do it on the board. They copy it and it slows them down usefully.
Also, Mira is ill. Somebody has to cover the nine o'clock.
Whoever is in the staff room at eight fifty-five is covering the nine o'clock.
That is the actual rule of this building and it's written nowhere.
I'll take it. What's her group doing?
Present perfect. There's a supply teacher coming Thursday, so leave them somewhere findable.
Is there a staff meeting this week?
Wednesday, thirty minutes, which historically means fifty.
And parents' evening is next week.
Six to eight, finishing at nine twenty. It's the end of term, so bring something to eat.
